strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/98be7f9b279a4cdab5a9db5bd11d308e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a simple, modular construction: forced exploration feeds change detectors, while an arbitrary stationary parametric-bandit algorithm handles exploitation and is restarted after detection.

The approach is practically intelligible and applies the same abstraction to linear, generalized-linear, and self-concordant bandits. Separating detector samples from the base algorithm also helps make the intended analysis modular.

The paper studies an important problem: adapting stationary bandit algorithms without knowing the number or locations of changes. A valid black-box reduction with preserved dimension dependence would be significant.

The experimental section covers three parametric-bandit families, abrupt and drifting changes, several relevant baselines, 30-run averages, and regimes with different expected numbers of changes. The figures consistently favor DAB in the tested synthetic settings.

Presentation is generally clear: the algorithm, regret decomposition, comparison table, and main experimental conclusions are easy to follow. No material research-ethics concern is apparent for these synthetic bandit experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—central detectability assumption: Equation (1) defines Δ_c as an infimum over every distinct θ,θ′ in Θ. For the norm-bounded continuous parameter sets subsequently claimed and used experimentally, this infimum is zero because θ′ can approach θ. Contrary to Section 3, choosing d linearly independent exploration actions does not make this infimum positive. Consequently the detector window and latency invoked in Theorem 1 need not be finite or O(log T), invalidating the stated optimal-regret conclusion for the advertised setting. A minimum jump-size/separated-parameter assumption—or a different analysis that charges undetected small changes by their regret—is essential.

Soundness—hidden dependence and overclaiming: the appendix acknowledges that m and ℓ depend on Δ_c, but then treats ℓ_D as O(log T) in Equation (22), suppressing the typically substantial inverse-gap dependence. The abstract, Table 1, and conclusion nevertheless advertise unconditional order-optimality under merely “mild” spacing assumptions. The result is instead restricted simultaneously by jump detectability and interval lengths large enough for forced samples to accumulate; these restrictions can exclude many legitimate piecewise-stationary instances and are not part of the cited minimax comparison.

Soundness—the general bound silently needs assumptions absent from Theorem 1. Equation (9) applies Jensen using concavity of R_B, although the theorem does not assume R_B is concave. There are also formal errors in the appendix: Equation (14) writes the observed pull count as no greater than the forced-pull indicator sum and then as no smaller than the resulting floor; the first inequality must be reversed. The first spacing condition in Theorem 1 also contains an unbound k. These may be repairable locally, but further reduce confidence in a proof supporting the main claim.

The claim of being the first feasible, optimal, prior-free black-box approach is insufficiently qualified. The proof is explicitly adapted from the modular detection analysis of Huang et al. (2025), and the substantive novelty over that framework is not sharply isolated. Feasibility is asserted without computational-complexity or runtime analysis of repeatedly maximizing the GLR statistic.

Experimental evidence is not reproducible from the paper. Exact values for α_0, detector thresholds and δ parameters, most base-algorithm settings, benchmark search spaces, tuning criteria, random seeds, and whether bands denote standard deviation, standard error, or confidence intervals are omitted. No code or supplementary reproducibility statement is provided. Saying ADA-OPKB was tuned “to optimize its performance” is also inadequate for assessing fair tuning.

The empirical evaluation does not test the assumptions driving the theorem: it reports neither realized jump sizes/Δ_c, spacing-condition violations, detection delays, false alarms, nor restart counts. There are no sensitivity studies for forced-exploration frequency or detector thresholds, ablations separating detection from exploration, runtime comparisons, or real/semi-real data. Thus the figures establish performance only for a narrow, heavily configured collection of synthetic instances.

The drifting-environment interpretation is speculative and partly inaccurate. In the random-walk experiment, an interior-ball increment ζ is centered rather than a deterministic “compounding bias”; its effects are stateful and temporally dependent, so they cannot simply be absorbed into independent observation noise. A single crossing plot against WeightUCB does not validate the broader claimed explanation or generalization to drifting environments.

Limitations are not treated adequately. Although the text notes that DAB is designed for sufficiently long stationary phases and can lose under faster drift, it does not disclose the fatal Δ_c=0 issue for continuous Θ, the strong quantitative separation requirement, tuning sensitivity, synthetic-only evaluation, or the absence of drift guarantees. Given that these limitations directly constrain the central optimality claim, the current manuscript requires a major theoretical and empirical revision before acceptance.

strengths: Originality/significance: The modular idea—combine forced exploration and per-action change detectors with an arbitrary stationary parametric-bandit algorithm—is simple, potentially useful, and covers linear, generalized-linear, and self-concordant bandits within one framework.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithm, and intended regret decomposition are generally clear. The paper explicitly discusses the minimum-spacing assumption and acknowledges that DAB is not theoretically designed for drifting environments.

Evidence: The experiments span three parametric-bandit families, several change frequencies, and 30-run averages. The additional random-walk experiment usefully identifies a regime in which DAB ceases to outperform WeightUCB.
Ethics: The work is theoretical and simulation-based, with no human-subject, privacy, or dataset concerns apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central definition of the detectable gap is incompatible with the claimed standard continuous parameter setting. For a norm-bounded continuum Θ and continuous mean function, Δ_c = inf_{θ≠θ'} max_{a∈A_e}|μ(<θ,a>)-μ(<θ',a>)| is zero because distinct parameters can be arbitrarily close. Contrary to Section 3, choosing linearly independent exploration actions does not make this infimum positive. Consequently, the claimed logarithmic detection latency, feasible separation condition, and dimension-only regret rates do not follow for the stated setting.

Soundness: The proof applies an ordinary expected stationary regret bound R_B after conditioning on the good detection event G (Eq. 9). Since G is determined by the same reward sequence, conditioning changes its distribution; an unconditional expected-regret guarantee for B cannot generally bound E[regret|G]. A high-probability guarantee or a different unconditional coupling argument is required. This is a material gap in the sole main theorem.

Soundness/significance: Change-detection delay necessarily depends on the jump magnitude, typically as Δ^{-2}. Property 1 and the final rate hide this dependence, while the comparison table reports only dimension, N_T, and T. Without a valid positive minimum-jump assumption, the advertised order-optimality and improvement for piecewise-stationary self-concordant bandits are unsupported.

Significance: The required spacing between changes scales with both detector latency and inverse forced-exploration frequency, yet the abstract and conclusion present the result broadly as optimal for piecewise-stationary parametric bandits. The manuscript neither establishes a corresponding lower bound for this restricted class nor carefully reconciles its restriction with the less constrained settings used in comparisons.

Evidence: The empirical study is limited to low-dimensional synthetic problems (d=5). It does not test the theorem's spacing condition, report detection delays or false-alarm rates, ablate forced exploration, vary dimension, or examine computational cost. Thus it does not validate the key theoretical mechanism or broad practical-feasibility claim.

Reproducibility: No code or complete hyperparameter specification is provided. Crucial choices—including α_0, detector thresholds, δ_F, δ_D, confidence parameters, and the exact baseline tuning procedure—are replaced by references to 'practical tuning' or tuning for best performance. The uncertainty bands are also not defined, and claims of significant improvement are made without statistical tests.

Presentation/limitations: The paper is readable, but it lacks a dedicated limitations discussion and does not acknowledge the zero-Δ_c issue, the jump-size dependence, or the conditional-expectation gap. Claims such as 'first,' 'order-optimal,' and 'significantly outperforms' are therefore substantially stronger than the supplied theory and experiments support.

Overall: The modular construction is promising, but the central theorem currently has a fundamental proof gap and relies on a detectability quantity that vanishes in the paper's stated continuous parameter model. These issues prevent the claimed contribution from being relied upon without major theoretical revision.

strengths: Originality/significance: DAB is a simple, modular wrapper combining forced exploration, per-action change detection, and restarts. Extending this black-box perspective across linear, generalized-linear, and self-concordant bandits is useful, and the potential improvement claimed for piecewise-stationary self-concordant bandits is particularly interesting.

Presentation: The motivation, algorithm, and decomposition of regret into false alarms, delayed detection, stationary learning, and forced exploration are generally clear. Table 1 usefully situates the claimed rates relative to prior work.

Empirical promise: Across the reported synthetic experiments, DAB consistently achieves lower dynamic regret than MASTER, WeightUCB, and, where applicable, ADA-OPKB. The inclusion of 30-run results for three parametric-bandit classes and both abrupt and drifting environments is valuable.

The paper openly acknowledges that its theorem requires sufficiently separated changes and that DAB is not theoretically designed for drifting environments; these honest qualifications should not be penalized.
Ethics: The work is theoretical and uses synthetic data, with no apparent human-subject, privacy, or immediate misuse concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive issue: The claimed order-optimal guarantee lacks a necessary minimum-change assumption. Equation (1) defines Δc as an infimum over every distinct θ,θ′ in Θ. For the continuous norm-bounded parameter sets used throughout the paper, arbitrarily close parameters normally make Δc=0. Consequently, the detector latency and pre-change window can be unbounded. The statement that d linearly independent exploration actions guarantee nonzero Δc is false without a finite or separated parameter class. This directly undermines the central order-optimality claim as currently stated.

The proof appears to apply the stationary algorithm's regret bound inside an expectation conditioned on the good detection event G (Equations (8)–(9)). Because G depends on observed rewards, conditioning changes their distribution; an ordinary expected-regret guarantee RB cannot automatically bound this conditional regret. The theorem would need a suitable pathwise/high-probability stationary guarantee or a different argument.

The proof invokes independence of rewards across time and actions in Equations (13) and (19), but the main problem statement only specifies zero-mean sub-Gaussian noise. These additional stochastic assumptions should be stated and their compatibility with the covered bandit models established.

Theorem 1 and its proof contain consequential notation or direction problems: k is undefined in the first spacing condition, and Equation (14) displays the detector sample count as no greater than the forced-exploration count even though the text and subsequent argument require the reverse inequality. These may be repairable, but they make the current proof difficult to verify reliably.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Numerical values for α0, detector thresholds and error probabilities, benchmark tuning ranges/procedures, initialization details, and the meaning of uncertainty bands are not reported; no code is provided. Saying that parameters follow another paper is insufficient to reconstruct the experiments, particularly when ADA-OPKB is explicitly tuned for the evaluation.

The empirical scope is narrow: all experiments use synthetic environments with d=5 and T=50,000, no sensitivity analysis for dimension, horizon, jump magnitude, noise, or exploration frequency, and no ablation separating forced exploration from detection and restarting. Claims of significant superiority are made without statistical tests or clearly defined confidence intervals.

The drifting-environment explanation is heuristic and somewhat misleading: a sequence of small, conditionally nonzero mean shifts cannot generally be 'absorbed' into zero-mean noise. Figure 5 is an informative observation, but it does not validate the broader claim that DAB bridges abrupt and drifting regimes.

Limitations are discussed informally, but the manuscript does not adequately acknowledge its dependence on detectable jump sizes, stochastic independence, computational costs of maintaining GLR tests, or benchmark-tuning sensitivity. Overall, the idea is promising, but the missing assumptions and conditional-regret proof gap require substantial revision before the main theorem can be relied upon.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: adapting stationary bandit algorithms to non-stationarity without knowing the number or magnitude of changes. The modular combination of a base learner, forced exploration, and a GLR detector is simple and potentially useful across linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, and kernel bandits.

The empirical scope is broad: four synthetic bandit classes, piecewise-stationary and drifting regimes, six data-derived benchmarks, multiple prior-free and prior-based baselines, and 15 runs. DAL appears consistently strong, and the paper appropriately includes a drift regime where WeightUCB eventually surpasses DAL rather than claiming universal dominance.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly explains the algorithmic intuition, relationship to detection-based MAB methods, and practical limitations of MASTER. Its limitations section honestly identifies the separation assumption and the lack of drifting-environment guarantees.

The work has moderate originality and significance: extending a detection/restart recipe to large or infinite action spaces through finite monitoring sets is an appealing idea, although much of the framework and regret template is inherited from prior change-detection bandit work.
No major research-ethics concern is apparent. The manuscript identifies the public or previously released datasets and notes the non-commercial use of Yahoo Finance data.
weaknesses: The central kernel-bandit theory is effectively vacuous. Proposition 4.2 assumes that, at one fixed action, inf_{f != f'} |f(a)-f'(a)| is strictly positive over an RKHS norm ball. For a continuous function class this infimum is zero: one can choose two arbitrarily close distinct functions, or functions differing elsewhere. Consequently, the proposition's premise generally cannot hold, and Corollary 4.4 does not substantiate the advertised improved PS-KB regret bound.

A related issue affects the detection argument more broadly: the defined discernibility quantity Delta_c takes an infimum over every distinct pair of admissible reward functions or parameters, so it is normally zero without a minimum jump-size restriction. The paper nonetheless describes logarithmic detection complexity and order-optimality without clearly stating such a restriction. The change-point spacing condition hides detector latency and window lengths that themselves depend on change magnitude, making the claim of a mild, roughly sqrt(T/k) separation condition misleading.

Theorem 4.3 is not established at an ICML-ready level. Its appendix gives only a short verbal claim that the result follows 'exactly' from another paper, without stating or checking the imported detector guarantees, distributions, bounded-regret assumptions, dependence on jump sizes, or correspondence between DAL's detection-indexed exploration schedule and the true change index. Since the headline improvements rely on this theorem, this is a major soundness problem.

The drifting analysis is only a heuristic plus one linear-bandit sweep. Treating small per-step drift as noise does not establish stationarity because the drift accumulates and changes the conditional mean. It therefore cannot support the paper's broader suggestion that piecewise-stationary methods bridge the two regimes.

The empirical evidence is less conclusive than its breadth suggests. Several 'real-world' evaluations are transformed or partly synthetic environments rather than online evaluations: Criteo rewards come from a fitted logistic model with synthetically injected sign changes, while logged click, stock, sensor, and advertisement records are converted into reward sequences. The paper does not discuss replay validity, selection bias, or how these constructions preserve the claimed parametric models.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or configuration archive is supplied; exact detector and baseline hyperparameters are replaced by references to prior recommendations or unspecified 'practical tuning'; Yahoo Finance tickers and retrieval dates are absent; preprocessing includes subjective filters; and the Yahoo rolling-average window is inconsistent between the main text (2000 rounds) and Appendix A.3 (100 rounds). Error bands are plotted but not defined, and numerical results or statistical comparisons are not reported.

The practical exploration setup is insufficiently explained. With Ne=100, T=50000, and the stated alpha_k=0.01*sqrt(k Ne log(T)/T), the initial exploration block can span more than the entire horizon before another forced-exploration cycle. Experiments additionally feed base-learner samples to the detector, unlike the stated algorithm. This discrepancy needs an explicit implementation and ablation showing whether gains arise from the claimed covering-set mechanism.

Presentation is polished overall, but some claims are overstated ('consistently surpasses,' 'order-optimal,' and improved best-known bounds) given the theoretical defects and evaluation design. The paper also lacks a dedicated ethics/data-governance discussion, though the apparent ethical risk is low.

strengths: Originality/significance: The modular combination of a stationary learner, forced exploration, and a change detector is simple and potentially useful across linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, and kernelized bandits.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates several bandit families, piecewise-stationary and drifting regimes, synthetic settings, and six data-derived benchmarks. The reported results are consistently favorable to DAL and include variability bands over 15 runs.

Presentation: The high-level motivation and Algorithm 1 are easy to follow. The paper also openly identifies the change-point separation requirement and lack of drifting-environment guarantees as limitations.
Ethics: The experiments use public or previously published datasets, and no clear material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The kernel-bandit theory rests on an effectively impossible assumption. Proposition 4.2 requires a point at which inf_{f != f'} |f(a)-f'(a)| is strictly positive over an RKHS norm ball. In a continuous function class, one can choose arbitrarily close distinct functions—and often distinct functions agreeing exactly at that point—so this infimum is zero. Consequently, Proposition 4.2 does not provide a usable covering construction, and the claimed improved PS-KB bound in Corollary 4.4 is unsupported. This is a central issue in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/218d3d490148433090371a694dd8975f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Soundness: The same problem appears in the definition of Delta_c as an infimum over every pair of distinct reward functions: for continuous parameter spaces it is generally zero. Although GLR sample complexity scales as 1/Delta_c^2, the main regret claim does not state a nonzero minimum-change assumption or expose this dependence. Instead, it hides detectability inside undefined quantities m_D and ell_D, so the advertised order-optimality is not established uniformly over the stated model.

Soundness/reproducibility: Theorem 4.3 receives only a short proof sketch saying it follows from another paper. The manuscript does not state the detector guarantee being imported, quantitatively define its latency and pre-change requirements, or verify that all assumptions remain valid under DAL's covering set, adaptive sampling, and restart schedule. This is inadequate support for the paper's principal theoretical claims.

Soundness: Proposition 4.1 incorrectly says that inner products with any maximal linearly independent subset of A uniquely determine theta. This holds only if span(A)=R^d. If not, they determine only the projection relevant to A; the proposition and proof need to be reformulated accordingly.

Empirical evidence: Several descriptions are internally inconsistent. The Yahoo experiment uses a rolling window of 2000 rounds and five days in the main text but 100 rounds and ten days in the appendix. The synthetic kernel setup simultaneously specifies ten-dimensional actions and an RKHS construction based on a one-dimensional discretization of [-1,1], without explaining how these objects are combined.

Empirical evidence/reproducibility: There is no code or complete configuration. Crucial GLR parameters, detector variances, baseline settings, ADA-OPKB tuning ranges, random seeds, and the meaning of uncertainty bands are omitted. DAL and ADA-OPKB also receive different descriptions of tuning access, preventing assessment of whether the comparisons are equitable.

Significance/evaluation: The so-called real-world experiments are mostly offline reward simulators built through extensive smoothing, filtering, rescaling, parameter estimation, and artificial change injection. Some preprocessing explicitly removes globally strong actions or actions that remain best for too long. These choices may favor detection-based restarting, and the paper provides neither ablations nor safeguards against full-dataset leakage.

Originality: The main regret analysis is presented as a direct adaptation of the modular MAB analysis in reference [27]. The genuinely new theoretical step is chiefly the construction of finite detection sets for broader bandit classes, but the kernel construction is vacuous and the parametric proof is misstated. This substantially reduces the supported novelty.

Limitations: The discussion acknowledges change-point spacing and the absence of drift theory, but not the more fundamental missing minimum-jump condition, the vacuity of the RKHS assumption, tuning sensitivity, or biases introduced by dataset preprocessing. Given these central technical and evidential problems, the work is not currently reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: Significance: DAL is a simple, practically useful wrapper combining forced exploration, change detection, and restarts with existing stationary bandit algorithms. Supporting parametric and kernelized bandits through one modular framework would be valuable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/b361cdc212ff469f87975ed56e4e45b0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Empirical breadth: the evaluation covers linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, and kernelized bandits; piecewise-stationary and drifting environments; synthetic experiments and six data-derived benchmarks; and several relevant prior-free and prior-based baselines. DAL performs consistently well in the reported results.

Presentation: the motivation, algorithm, and relationship among the detector, exploration schedule, and stationary learner are clearly explained. Figures are legible, and the paper is generally polished and easy to follow.

Originality: although detection-based restarting and GLR tests are established, extending the modular construction to large or infinite action spaces through finite detecting sets is an interesting direction with moderate novelty.

The authors appropriately acknowledge important limitations, including the change-point separation assumption and the absence of a drifting-environment regret guarantee. These honest disclosures should not themselves be penalized.
No unresolved major ethical concern is apparent. The experiments primarily use synthetic or public data, and the Yahoo Finance use is identified as non-commercial academic research.
weaknesses: Soundness, decisively: the kernel-bandit theory relies on an apparently vacuous assumption. Proposition 4.2 assumes an action at which the infimum of |f(a)-f'(a)| over distinct norm-bounded RKHS functions is greater than a positive quantity. In a continuous RKHS class, one can generally take f' arbitrarily close to f, making this infimum zero. Consequently, Proposition 4.2 does not establish a useful detecting set for the stated function class, and Corollary 4.4's claimed improved PS-KB regret bound is unsupported as written.

The same quantitative issue appears in the definition of the detection gap Delta_c: an infimum over all distinct admissible reward functions or parameters is normally zero. Proposition 4.1 only proves qualitative identifiability and ignores basis conditioning, link sensitivity, observation noise, and jump magnitude. An arbitrary linearly independent set can make a change nearly undetectable. These quantities directly determine GLR sample complexity and cannot simply be hidden in an unspecified spacing condition while claiming uniform order-optimality.

Theorem 4.3 receives only a short proof sketch asserting that a prior MAB theorem applies after replacing the number of arms by the covering-set size. The detector latency and pre-change sample requirements are left abstract, their dependence on change magnitude is not incorporated into the displayed regret bound, and the indexing of the exploration rates versus true and detected changes is not justified. Given that the strongest theoretical claims depend on this transfer, a complete proof is needed.

The empirical evidence is broad but not sufficiently diagnostic. There are no ablations for forced exploration, detector choice, exploration frequency, or the strength of the selected stationary base learner. Thus, it is unclear how much of the improvement comes from DAL itself versus choices such as REDS or OFUGLB. Numerical result tables and clearly defined uncertainty intervals or statistical comparisons are also absent.

Baseline tuning is insufficiently documented. ADA-OPKB is explicitly tuned to optimize evaluation performance, while other methods use vaguely described recommended parameters; the information provided to prior-based baselines is not stated. Detector tuning is deferred to another work without reporting the final values. This prevents assessment of fairness and sensitivity.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or complete configurations are supplied, data filtering includes subjective steps such as removing high-value or frequently optimal actions, and important descriptions conflict. For example, Yahoo CTR smoothing uses a 2000-round window in Section 3.2 but a 100-round window in Appendix A.3; the Criteo appendix also says 60% of coordinates are flipped at each time step despite the main text describing geometric change points.

The so-called real-world experiments are mostly constructed offline environments based on heavily smoothed, filtered, fitted, or otherwise transformed traces. They do not constitute online logged-policy replay or deployment evidence, so claims about performance in real-world scenarios should be qualified.

The discussion of drifting environments is heuristic rather than theoretically sound: treating a small, persistent parameter drift as zero-mean noise is generally invalid because it induces structured bias that accumulates over time. Figure 3 illustrates a phenomenon but does not validate the proposed explanation.

Originality is limited by the framework's close conceptual dependence on existing forced-exploration plus GLR-restart methods. The paper needs a valid and quantitatively developed large-action-space theory to make the extension a sufficiently strong contribution.

The limitations section does not identify the vacuity of the uniform separation assumption, reproducibility gaps, sensitivity to costly or unsafe forced exploration, or potential feedback and fairness concerns in recommendation and advertising deployments. These are relevant practical limitations, though they do not create a material ethical bar by themselves.

strengths: Originality/significance: DAL is an appealing modular recipe—periodic forced exploration, change detection, and restart of an arbitrary stationary learner—and its unification of linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, kernelized, and contextual bandits could be practically useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/3a8f4c622d3e47bfbb6bd82f4d643344/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Empirical scope: the paper evaluates five bandit families, piecewise-stationary and drifting settings, several strong baselines, 15 trials, and nine synthetic or data-derived benchmarks. This is unusually broad for the area.

Presentation: the high-level motivation and algorithm are generally easy to follow, and the paper clearly explains the roles of the detector, covering set, forced exploration, and stationary base learner.

Limitations: the authors appropriately acknowledge the change-point separation assumption and absence of drifting-regime guarantees; these disclosures are useful and should not themselves count against the work.
weaknesses: Soundness—the kernel result rests on an effectively vacuous assumption. Proposition 4.2 requires inf over every pair of distinct RKHS functions of their difference at one fixed action to be strictly positive. For the stated RKHS norm ball, arbitrarily close distinct functions exist, so this infimum is zero. Consequently, the proposed covering construction does not establish a usable uniform detection gap, and the advertised improved PS-KB guarantee cannot generally be instantiated.

Soundness—the contextual-bandit proof appears incorrect. In Appendix B.4, the complement of an event quantified over all earlier segments is replaced by an event involving only the latest segment without justification. More seriously, the asserted Chernoff bound exp(-2 m_D (log T)^2) does not follow from an interval providing roughly log T + m_D/s context opportunities: the expected margin above m_D is only s log T, and the concentration exponent must depend on s and the number of trials. This undermines the claimed T^-2 failure probability and hence the general PS-CB theorem.

Soundness/general claims: the paper defines a uniform discernibility gap as an infimum over distinct reward functions, but this gap is also zero for ordinary continuous parametric classes unless a minimum change magnitude is imposed. The theorem instead hides jump dependence inside detector latency and window quantities without clearly stating the required jump-size assumptions. Thus the description of the assumptions as mild and the broad order-optimality claims are not adequately supported.

Algorithmic specification: the prescribed exploration frequency can exceed one for sufficiently large restart index, contradicting the earlier requirement that it lie in (0,1) and making the exploration schedule invalid unless it is clipped. No clipping or corresponding analysis is given. The manuscript also has repeated theorem-number mismatches: the appendix claims to prove Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4, while the main results are Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5.

Evaluation/reproducibility: DAL is called hyperparameter-free, yet its results depend on detector false-alarm/missed-detection settings, Gaussian variance, covering-set construction, and base-learner choices. The exact detector tuning, baseline search spaces and selected values, uncertainty definition, and many preprocessing thresholds are absent. No code is provided, and the new microarchitecture dataset is only promised for future release. Several preprocessing descriptions use non-operational choices such as removing stocks with 'extremely high' statistics or filtering high-noise and persistently optimal actions.

Empirical validity: many 'real-world' experiments are heavily synthesized rather than faithful online evaluations. Criteo uses fitted logistic rewards with artificial parameter flips; Yahoo R6A applies extensive smoothing, filtering, scaling, and time compression; and the COVID benchmark mixes two clinical endpoints and deterministically concatenates successes and failures. For logged-feedback datasets such as Zozo, the counterfactual evaluation protocol is not sufficiently specified. These constructions may still be benchmarks, but they do not justify strong claims of demonstrated real-world effectiveness.

Experimental evidence is incomplete: the paper gives curves but no numerical result table, statistical tests, detector diagnostics, restart counts, computational comparison, sensitivity analysis, or ablations for covering-set size and forced-exploration rate. Baselines are tuned for best performance without reporting how, making the claimed consistent superiority difficult to audit.

Presentation and ethics: despite readable exposition, key definitions and proof dependencies are deferred to recent external work, and the main new theorem receives only a sketch. The paper does not discuss limitations of using retrospective clinical, advertising, and financial data as decision-making benchmarks, possible selection bias introduced by preprocessing, or deployment risks. No acute ethical violation is evident, but the treatment is insufficient for the application-facing claims. Overall, these central theoretical errors and reproducibility gaps outweigh the promising framework and require a reject rather than a borderline recommendation.

strengths: The modular idea—combining a stationary bandit learner, forced exploration, and a GLR change detector—is simple, broadly relevant, and potentially useful in practice.
The paper attempts unusually broad coverage across linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, kernelized, and contextual bandits, with both piecewise-stationary and drifting experiments.

The experimental section includes many synthetic and data-derived environments, multiple prior-free and prior-based baselines, 15 trials for the reported plots, and useful implementation and hardware information in the appendix.
The manuscript is generally readable and openly acknowledges two important limitations: the change-point separation assumption and the lack of drifting-regime guarantees.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central detection assumption is generally untenable as written. The paper defines a uniform separation via an infimum over every distinct pair of reward functions. For continuous parameter or RKHS classes this infimum is normally zero because distinct functions can be arbitrarily close. Proposition 4.2 assumes that this infimum at one action is strictly larger than 2BL_u delta_T, which is impossible for the usual RKHS ball and can also fail because two distinct functions may agree at that action. Proposition 4.1 establishes only identifiability/nonzero change, not the uniform effect size needed for logarithmic detection delay. Consequently, the claimed general order-optimal guarantees and improved PS-KB/PS-SCB bounds do not follow without a substantive minimum-change assumption.

Soundness: the contextual-bandit claim is much narrower than advertised. DAL stores a separate history for every exact context-action pair and the theorem assumes a finite context set with a positive minimum occurrence probability s. This does not cover standard contextual bandits with continuous, large, or nonrepeating contexts, despite repeated claims of applicability to general contextual bandits.

Soundness: the contextual theorem proof is only a sketch and contains apparent invalid steps. In Appendix B.4, an event involving a union over all prior segments is replaced by an event for only the most recent segment. The subsequent Chernoff exponent does not follow from the stated sample count, especially when s is small. The appendix also alternates between log(T) and 2log(T) in the required spacing. These issues leave the main theorem unestablished.

Soundness/presentation: the exploration rate alpha_k can exceed one for allowed k even though the algorithm requires alpha_k in (0,1); no clipping or additional restriction is supplied. The GLR pseudocode takes delta_D as input but never uses it. The text also misnumbers Theorem 4.4 as Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.5 as Corollary 4.4 throughout the appendix.

Evidence: the claim of consistent superiority is not supported by sufficiently controlled comparisons. Baseline tuning is described only as optimizing performance, DAL's practical detector parameters are deferred vaguely to prior work, and neither tuning grids nor complete selected values are reported. The figures provide no numerical result tables or statistical tests, and uncertainty reporting is inconsistent or difficult to interpret.

Evidence: many purported real-world evaluations are heavily engineered simulations rather than faithful online benchmarks. Yahoo R6A uses smoothing, thresholding, removal of globally strong or persistent-best actions, horizon compression, and a tenfold CTR rescaling; Criteo fits a logistic model and injects synthetic changes; the clinical data are converted into a deterministic sequence by concatenating successes and failures in an arbitrary fixed order. Such constructions can favor restart-based detection and do not substantiate broad real-world effectiveness.

Evidence: the Yahoo R6B protocol selects its Top-K vocabulary using the evaluation window and reports unweighted indicator-matched reward. This creates data leakage and is not a clearly justified replay/IPS estimator when candidate-set sizes vary. The clinical benchmark also combines survival and improvement as separate observations and aggregates heterogeneous treatments without discussing clinical validity, making practical conclusions especially questionable.

Reproducibility: no code or complete configuration is provided. Several preprocessing details and filters are underspecified, and the manuscript contains contradictions: Yahoo R6A uses a 2000-round rolling average in the main text but 100 rounds in the appendix; Criteo changes are described as geometric change-points but Appendix A.3 says 60% of coordinates change at every time step. The novel prefetcher series is currently unavailable and explicitly cannot be reconstructed without the authors' stack.

Significance/originality: GLR-triggered restarts with forced exploration already underpin the closest cited work. The main novelty is breadth of application, but the crucial extensions either require restrictive finite-context and detectability assumptions or lack a valid proof. Thus the submission does not currently establish the claimed general black-box advance.

Ethics/limitations: there is no meaningful discussion of risks from interpreting synthetic stock, advertising, or especially clinical-treatment benchmarks as evidence of deployable decision-making. Dataset licensing is only partly addressed, and promising future release of an unreproducible dataset is insufficient for present evaluation.

strengths: The modular idea—augmenting a stationary bandit learner with forced exploration and change detection—is practically appealing and is presented clearly in Algorithm 1.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, kernelized, and contextual bandits under both abrupt changes and drift, with 15 trials and several real-data-derived benchmarks.

The paper is generally readable and provides useful implementation and preprocessing detail in the appendix. Its discussion honestly acknowledges the lack of drifting-regime guarantees and the change-point separation requirement.

The cross-setting synthesis, new benchmark constructions, and attempt to translate stationary regret guarantees into non-stationary ones constitute potentially significant contributions. No major research-ethics concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims are not supported as stated. Detection complexity depends on the inverse squared change magnitude, yet Theorem 4.4 imposes no quantitative minimum jump and omits this dependence from the regret. Merely establishing that some monitored mean changes by a nonzero amount does not yield logarithmic detection delay or a uniform order-optimal bound.

The kernel-bandit result relies on Proposition 4.2's assumption that inf_{f≠f'} |f(a)-f'(a)| is strictly positive over an RKHS norm ball. This is impossible for the stated continuous function class: two distinct admissible functions can be arbitrarily close. Moreover, the proof only obtains a strictly positive residual change, not the lower bound needed to control GLR latency. Consequently, the claimed improved PS-KB bound is effectively based on a vacuous assumption.

The contextual-bandit proof contains a substantive concentration gap. Equation (7) claims a failure probability exp(-2 m_D (log T)^2) from only about m_D/s+log T scheduled opportunities with context probability at least s; standard Hoeffding/Chernoff calculations do not give that exponent or the asserted T^{-2} bound. Several indices in this derivation are also inconsistent. This undermines the PS-CB guarantee.

The claimed state-of-the-art improvements are not compared under clearly matched assumptions. DAL requires detectable changes and sufficiently separated change points, whereas cited adaptive bounds can apply without these detection conditions. Describing the resulting SCB and KB rates as unconditional improvements is therefore misleading.

The drifting results are empirical and heuristic only. A single additional linear-bandit sweep does not validate the broad claim that piecewise-stationary methods bridge drifting regimes, and the paper identifies no measurable condition under which DAL should outperform drift-specific algorithms.

The evaluation does not provide numerical result tables, uncertainty estimates for final comparisons, statistical tests, detector/covering-set ablations, or sensitivity analyses. Baseline tuning spaces and selected values are omitted, while DAL's detector tuning is deferred to prior work; thus the across-the-board superiority visible in plots is difficult to audit.

Some 'real-world' evaluations are heavily constructed simulations. Yahoo R6A uses centered smoothing and extensive action filtering; Criteo fits a model and injects artificial changes; the COVID benchmark deterministically concatenates aggregated successes and failures. For Yahoo R6B, the vocabulary is selected on the evaluation window and the reported replay formula lacks explicit propensity correction despite varying candidate sets. These choices raise leakage and counterfactual-validity concerns that are not analyzed.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the breadth of the claims: no code is identified, random seeds and hyperparameter-search protocols are absent, several preprocessing filters have unspecified thresholds, and the prefetcher data is only promised for future release.

The descriptions 'black-box' and 'hyperparameter-free' are overstated. DAL requires a finite covering set with structural knowledge, detector thresholds and distribution/noise choices, the horizon, and a finite-context/minimum-context-probability condition for its contextual theory. The prescribed exploration frequency can also exceed its declared range (0,1) without an explicit cap.

Presentation has avoidable technical inconsistencies: the appendix proves Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 although the main text labels them Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5, and the theoretical appendix largely supplies a sketch referring to prior work rather than a self-contained proof of the main generalization. These issues compound the difficulty of verifying the contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: DAL is a simple, potentially useful modular recipe—forced exploration, change detection, and restarting—that extends detection-based ideas beyond multi-armed bandits to several structured and contextual settings.

Empirical breadth: the paper evaluates linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, kernelized, and contextual bandits on synthetic scenarios and nine data-derived benchmarks, comparing against several prior-free and prior-based baselines. Runtime measurements are also included.

Presentation: the motivation and high-level algorithm are generally clear, and the figures and tables are legible. The appendix provides preprocessing descriptions and a substantial proof attempt rather than omitting technical details.

Limitations/ethics: the paper honestly acknowledges the change-point separation requirement and absence of drifting-regime guarantees. The datasets are mostly public or aggregate, so the immediate ethical risk appears limited.
weaknesses: Soundness—detectability assumptions: the central order-optimality claim suppresses essential dependence on change magnitude. Property 4.1 states logarithmic detection latency without the usual inverse-squared jump dependence, although the text itself acknowledges this dependence. For continuous parameter classes, the defined infimum over all distinct reward functions is generally zero. Most seriously, Proposition 4.3 assumes inf_{f != f'} |f(a)-f'(a)| > L_T over an RKHS ball, which is impossible for a nontrivial continuous class because arbitrarily close distinct functions exist. Consequently, the advertised kernelized guarantee is effectively vacuous, and the broad minimax/order-optimality claims are unsupported without an explicit minimum-jump assumption and its regret dependence.

Soundness—contextual scope: the model permits changes in the context distribution P_t, but DAL monitors conditional reward means only. A pure change in P_t need not trigger any detector, while it can change the best policy for a restricted policy class. The contextual proof instead selects a context-action pair whose reward changes, so it does not establish the theorem for the stated model.

Soundness—contextual rate: Theorem 4.8 contains an additional sqrt(|C| N_e N_T T) exploration term. Corollary 4.9 absorbs it by asserting |Pi|=|A|^{|C|}, which holds only for the universal policy class, not for the arbitrary policy class used in the theorem and Table 1. Thus the claimed general contextual-bandit rate does not follow. Dependence on the minimum context probability s is also hidden through the separation requirement and can be severe.

Evidence: the paper repeatedly claims consistent state-of-the-art superiority, but provides curves without numerical summaries, confidence intervals for many real-data plots, significance tests, or adequate sensitivity studies. Only 15 trials are used. There is no ablation isolating forced exploration, detector choice, restart behavior, covering-set selection, or the finite-action modification in Remark 3.1.

Evaluation validity: several “real-world” environments are heavily reconstructed or semi-synthetic. Criteo rewards come from a fitted logistic model with artificially flipped parameters; Yahoo R6A is extensively smoothed and filtered, including removal of arms that remain optimal too often; COVID outcomes are deterministically concatenated; and the R6B metric is described as unbiased IPS although the displayed estimator lacks propensity weighting. These choices may favor detectable mean shifts and do not convincingly establish real deployment performance.

Reproducibility: no code or complete configuration is supplied. Exact baseline hyperparameters and tuning ranges are absent, some preprocessing uses subjective filters such as removing “extremely” volatile stocks, and the prefetcher dataset is unavailable and explicitly said to be unreproducible from the description. The “hyperparameter-free” characterization is also overstated because DAL requires a detector/model choice, horizon, noise/KL specification, covering-set construction, and stationary learner.

Presentation: important conditions are described as “mild” or relegated to hidden constants despite being decisive. The appendix also contains indexing and inequality inconsistencies, and the PB/KB proof is largely deferred to a cited MAB result with the assertion that replacing the number of arms by the covering-set size suffices.

Research ethics: the generic impact statement does not discuss risks from applying non-stationary bandits to clinical treatment or advertising, including unsafe exploration, distribution shift, privacy, and fairness. This is not the primary rejection reason, but a stronger domain-specific limitations discussion is warranted.

strengths: The core idea is simple and potentially useful: periodically explore an informative action set, apply a change detector, and restart an arbitrary stationary bandit learner after detection. The modular presentation makes the proposed algorithm easy to understand.

The empirical study is unusually broad in scope, covering parametric, kernelized, self-concordant, and contextual bandits; synthetic piecewise-stationary and drifting environments; nine real-data-derived benchmarks; multiple baselines; and runtime measurements.
The paper is generally polished and well organized. It states the change-point separation assumption explicitly and acknowledges that the drifting-regime results lack theoretical guarantees.
The appendix provides substantial dataset-preprocessing detail and reports 15 independent runs for the main experiments.
weaknesses: The central order-optimality claim omits essential dependence on change magnitude. Property 4.1 asserts logarithmic detector sample complexity, but GLR/GSR latency necessarily scales with the inverse squared mean shift. The paper defines this dependence through Δ_c and then drops it from Theorem 4.8, Assumption 4.6, and the final regret bounds. For continuous parametric classes, infimum over distinct parameters gives Δ_c=0 because two parameters can be arbitrarily close; Proposition 4.2 guarantees only a nonzero monitored change, not one bounded away from zero. Consequently, the stated uniform order-optimal guarantee is unsupported without a minimum-jump assumption and corresponding latency/separation factors.

The kernelized result has an especially problematic premise: Proposition 4.3 assumes inf_{f≠f'} |f(a)-f'(a)|>L_T at some action over the RKHS norm ball. Such a class contains arbitrarily close distinct functions, so this infimum is zero. Thus the assumption is generally impossible as stated, making the claimed improved PS-KB bound effectively vacuous unless the function class or realized changes are explicitly separated.

The claimed general contextual-bandit applicability is not established. Algorithm 1 maintains a separate detector history for every exact context-action pair, while the proof requires a finite context set with positive minimum occurrence probability s. This excludes ordinary continuous or rarely repeated contexts. The Yahoo R6B experiment uses feature vectors from logged events that are likely distinct, but the manuscript does not explain how the per-context detector can collect pre- and post-change samples there. This creates a serious mismatch between the stated algorithm, theorem, and flagship real-world contextual experiment.

The 'prior-free' and 'hyperparameter-free' claims are overstated. The prescribed exploration rate depends on T, |C|, and N_e; the theoretical detector settings require δ_F=δ_D=T^{-η} with η>1, whereas experiments use δ_F=1/sqrt(T); and no experimental δ_D is specified. Moreover, α_k is declared to lie in (0,1), but its formula can exceed one for large |C|N_e or k, with no clipping rule or analysis.

The empirical evidence is weaker than the breadth suggests. Several 'real-world' tasks are heavily constructed simulations: Criteo rewards are regenerated from a fitted logistic model with artificial geometric changes, stock rewards receive synthetic noise, and Yahoo R6A is smoothed, segmented, filtered, and post-processed to remove persistently strong actions. The COVID benchmark concatenates deterministic endpoint counts, but the manuscript does not clearly define counterfactual rewards for actions not represented at a given round. These constructions do not by themselves substantiate strong claims of real-world effectiveness.

Results are presented almost entirely as crowded learning curves, without numerical summaries, confidence intervals defined in the text, statistical tests, detector diagnostics, ablations of forced exploration or covering-set choice, or sensitivity to thresholds and change magnitudes. The paper says some baselines are tuned for best performance while others use original hyperparameters, but gives insufficient search spaces and selected values to assess fairness.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the empirical claim: no implementation or code link is supplied, one novel dataset is only promised for future release, exact reconstruction of that benchmark is admitted to be infeasible, and many preprocessing and baseline-implementation choices remain underspecified.

Originality is moderate rather than commensurate with the claims. The framework is largely an extension of existing detection-and-restart methods, and the appendix states that the parametric and kernelized proof follows prior MAB results with the number of arms replaced by N_e. The genuinely broader reduction would still be valuable if correct, but the missing jump dependence and contextual limitations undermine that contribution.

The limitations discussion acknowledges separation and the absence of drifting guarantees, but not the more fundamental minimum-change and finite-context restrictions. The generic impact statement also overlooks the risks of interpreting highly simplified clinical and recommendation benchmarks as evidence for deployment. Overall, the attractive idea and extensive experiments do not compensate for unsupported central theoretical claims and unresolved evaluation/reproducibility issues in the manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/8eb16dfb356f4eb58237174100997072/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

strengths: The modular idea—combining forced exploration, a change detector, and an arbitrary stationary learner—is simple, practically appealing, and potentially useful across several bandit families.

The experimental scope is unusually broad, covering linear, generalized-linear, self-concordant, kernelized, and contextual bandits, with synthetic tests, nine real-data-derived benchmarks, runtime measurements, two detectors, and 15 trials.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly distinguishes the detector, covering set, exploration schedule, and stationary learner. It also gives algorithms, preprocessing descriptions, hardware information, and substantial appendices.

The work offers a meaningful extension of detection-based restarting beyond multi-armed bandits. The covering-set perspective provides useful insight into how structural complexity can make model-change detection feasible in large or continuous action spaces.

The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges the change-point separation assumption, lack of drifting-regime guarantees, and difficulty reproducing the microarchitecture dataset. No acute ethical concern is apparent from the described use of public or research datasets.
weaknesses: The central regret theorem is not supported by the stated exploration schedule. Theorem 4.8 sets alpha_k=sqrt(k|C|N_e/(2 sqrt(T) log^2 T)); consequently, the forced-exploration term alpha_bar T in Eq. (24) scales as T^(3/4)sqrt(|C|N_eN_T), rather than the claimed sqrt(|C|N_eN_T T). The surrounding statement that separation scales as approximately sqrt(T/k) also suggests that T, not sqrt(T), may have been intended in the denominator. Even if typographical, this error occurs in the theorem, experiments, and proof of a central claim.

The kernelized-bandit result relies on an apparently vacuous separation premise. Proposition 4.3 assumes that, at one action, inf_{f != f'} |f(a)-f'(a)| exceeds a positive L_T over an RKHS ball. For the stated continuous RKHS class, arbitrarily close distinct functions exist, making this infimum zero. Thus the advertised general PS-KB improvement does not follow without defining a discretely separated environment class or a minimum jump assumption and tracking its dependence.

The paper overstates generality for contextual bandits. Algorithm 1 maintains a detector for every exact context-action pair, and the proof assumes a finite context set with minimum positive mass s. This does not cover the usual continuous or large-context setting suggested by the phrase “general bandits,” and the resulting dependence on rare contexts can make the separation condition extremely demanding.

Several real-world evaluations do not establish a valid counterfactual bandit environment. In particular, the Yahoo R6B description calls the estimator IPS but reports sum_t 1{a_t=j_t}r_t without inverse-propensity weighting; action selection is also based on CTRs from the evaluation window. For the clinical, Bioliq, and Zozo logs, it is unclear how rewards for actions not selected in the source data are obtained. Consequently, the claim of consistent superiority on real-world problems is not yet adequately supported.

The evaluation lacks numerical result tables, uncertainty or significance reporting for several real-data plots, ablations of forced exploration and covering-set choice, and sensitivity analysis for the theoretically prescribed exploration rate and detector thresholds. Comparability is also difficult to assess because exact baseline hyperparameters and non-stationarity priors are not reported.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate for an empirical paper of this scope: no code or complete configuration is provided, some preprocessing rules are subjective or underspecified, and the microarchitecture dataset is unavailable at submission time. The generic impact statement also misses an opportunity to discuss risks of deploying restart-based adaptive decision systems in clinical or recommendation settings.
